description.describe_ch: 本課程主要目的為加強英文閱讀訓練。課堂上協助同學接觸各種商用英文書報資訊，透過閱讀相關商用報刊及雜誌，培養基礎英文書寫能力，深化英語閱讀、口說、與聽力的技能。教師引導同學認識並討論各項國貿商用議題，培養學生在職場所需之口語及書寫溝通技巧，能撰寫與職場相關之英文文件，並使用英文進行有效且適當的溝通。
description.describe_eh: The main purpose of this course is to strengthen English reading training. , students are assisted in accessing various business English books and newspapers. By reading relevant business newspapers and magazines, develop basic English writing skills, deepen their English reading, speaking, and listening skills. Teachers guide students to understand and discuss various international business issues, and develop their oral and writing skills in the workplace, enable to write documents and communicate effectively in English.

textBooks.tpb_book_en:
"The Economist" 2026
Aviation
A bumpy ascent
A record year for airlines is not what it seems
ROVANIEMI AIRPORT in Finland, gateway to the home of Father Christmas in Lapland, surpassed 1m arrivals for the first time in 2025.
Airlines serving fans of reindeer and ice swimming are not the only ones breaking records.
In 2025 the industry’s net profits will have hit an all-time high of nearly $40bn globally, reckons IATA, a trade group, far exceeding 2019’s pre-pandemic total of $26bn.
Yet plenty of challenges remain.
In 2024 they flew 4.8bn passengers, cruising past the previous peak reached in 2019.
In 2025 that figure probably reached 5bn.
For the first time combined revenues are expected to have exceeded $1trn.
As demand continued to run ahead of
additional capacity, load factors (a measure of seats filled) also hit a record, averaging nearly 84%, and should rise higher still in 2026.
Not everything has been in the ascent. European and North American airlines, which account for three-fifths of the industry’s net profits, have had to contend with circuitous long-haul routes to avoid Russian airspace since the start of the war in Ukraine.
This year parts of the Middle East became no-go zones after Israel’s strike on Iran in June.
America’s airlines were hit by a government shutdown that stopped federal workers from travelling and kept unpaid air-traffic controllers at home, disrupting flights.
What is more, despite a drop in fuel prices, which account for 25–30% of airlines’ operating expenses, other costs have risen.
This is mostly the result of a shortage of new aircraft.
Airlines may have recovered since the pandemic, but Boeing and Airbus are still under strain.
The aircraft duopoly’s combined deliveries of under 1,400 new planes in 2025 were some way off the record of just over 1,600 in 2018.
Boeing has struggled to increase its production ever since two fatal crashes of 737 MAX short-haul aircraft in late 2018 and early 2019 led to a 20-month grounding.
It has continued to struggle with quality control; in early 2024 a fuselage panel on another 737 MAX blew off mid-air.
Airbus, meanwhile, has had troubles of its own.
In early December it cut its target for deliveries for the year, from 820 planes to 790, as a result of a production flaw at a supplier of fuselage panels.
Ongoing trouble with suppliers, which scaled back during the pandemic and have had trouble scaling back up, may continue to disrupt plane-making.
Problems with some Pratt & Whitney engines have led to the grounding of a third of the global fleet of Airbus’s A320neo single-aisle jets.
The resulting shortfall in the supply of aircraft is unlikely to be resolved before 2031 at the earliest, according to IATA.
Fuel efficiency, maintenance costs and emissions have all suffered as carriers have been forced to keep older planes in the air for longer.
The average age of the global fleet is around 15 years, compared with 13 years in 2019.
In the past fuel efficiency tended to improve by around 2% a year as new planes came into service, but this slowed to 0.3% in 2025.
A recent report by IATA and Oliver Wyman, a consultancy, estimates that the cost to the airline industry of its ageing fleet, including extra fuel, repairs and spare parts, was over $11bn in 2025.
Moreover, some airlines are failing to expand their routes as fast as planned owing to a lack of available aircraft.
Thus, despite their record year, airlines still eked out only a meagre net margin of 4%, equivalent to just $7.90 of profit per passenger.
The industry’s bosses should not be celebrating just yet.

weeklyScds.tpd_reading_en:
Unit 1 Topic: Global Aviation and International Trade
Reading:
The Economist (January 3rd, 2026)
“A Record Year for Airlines Is Not What It Seems”
Learning Instructions:
Students should read the assigned article before class and identify key vocabulary related to aviation, tourism, and global trade. Students should underline unfamiliar words and summarize the main argument using the 5W1H framework (Who, What, When, Where, Why, and How). Students are encouraged to think about how aviation connects different regions of the world and supports international mobility and trade flows.
weeklyScds.tpd_ass_en:
Pre-class preparation:
1. Read the assigned Economist article.
2. Identify key vocabulary related to aviation and international trade.
3. Prepare a short summary of the article using the 5W1H framework.

In-class learning activities:
1. Lecture on global aviation and its role in international trade.
2. Vocabulary explanation and reading guidance.
3. Group discussion on how aviation supports global economic activity.
4. Student reflection on how air transport connects tourism, trade, and globalization.

weeklyScds.tpd_reading_en:
Unit 2
Intellectual Property and Globalisation
Reading
The Economist (2026)
Copycat Crisis
weeklyScds.tpd_ass_en:
Learning Instructions
Students will explore the relationship between intellectual property protection and global trade. Before class, students should read the article and identify examples of counterfeit goods and intellectual property disputes. Students should consider how globalization increases both innovation and the risk of imitation.
Preliminary Homework
Read the assigned article.
Identify examples of intellectual property conflicts.
List unfamiliar vocabulary related to patents and trademarks.
Learning Activities
Lecture on intellectual property rights in global trade.
Discussion on counterfeit products and globalization.
Case discussion on international IP disputes.
Student reflections on innovation protection.

weeklyScds.tpd_reading_en:
Semiconductors and Global Technology Supply Chains
Reading
The Economist (February 2026)
Elbow Grease (Arm & AI chips)
weeklyScds.tpd_ass_en:
Learning Instructions
Students should read the article and identify how semiconductor design companies such as Arm influence global technology supply chains. Students are encouraged to analyze how artificial intelligence and chip development shape international trade and digital industries.
Preliminary Homework
Read the article before class.
Identify key companies mentioned in the semiconductor industry.
List important technical vocabulary.

Learning Activities
Lecture on global semiconductor supply chains.
Vocabulary explanation related to technology industries.
Group discussion on AI chips and international trade.
Short reflection on technology competition.

weeklyScds.tpd_reading_en:
Artificial Intelligence and the Future of Smartphones
Reading
The Economist
Will AI Replace the Smartphone?
weeklyScds.tpd_ass_en:
Learning Instructions

Students will explore emerging technologies and their impact on digital markets. Students should consider how artificial intelligence may transform the current smartphone ecosystem.

Preliminary Homework

Read the article and highlight key arguments.

Identify examples of AI-driven devices.

Prepare discussion points about future digital technologies.

Learning Activities

Lecture on digital innovation and global markets.

Vocabulary explanation related to artificial intelligence.

Group discussion on future consumer technology.

Student reflections on technological change.

weeklyScds.tpd_reading_en:
Emerging Multinational Corporations
Reading
The Economist
China’s New Multinationals
weeklyScds.tpd_ass_en:
Learning Instructions

Students should analyze how emerging market firms expand internationally. The article introduces the rise of Chinese multinational corporations and their role in global markets.

Preliminary Homework

Read the article before class.

Identify examples of multinational companies.

List vocabulary related to international business expansion.

Learning Activities

Lecture on multinational enterprises.

Discussion on global business expansion.

Case analysis of emerging multinational firms.

Student reflections on global competition.

weeklyScds.tpd_reading_en:
Global Finance and Exchange Rate Risks
Reading
The Economist
Financial Markets – The Dangerous Dollar
weeklyScds.tpd_ass_en:
Learning Instructions

Students will examine the role of exchange rates in global financial markets. Students should analyze how fluctuations in the US dollar affect international trade and capital flows.

Preliminary Homework

Read the article and identify the main economic arguments.

List vocabulary related to exchange rates and finance.

Prepare short notes on global currency risks.

Learning Activities

Lecture on global financial markets.

Vocabulary explanation related to finance.

Group discussion on exchange rate impacts.

Student reflections on financial globalization.

weeklyScds.tpd_reading_en:
Innovation and Business Strategy
Reading
The Economist – Schumpeter Column
Back to the Future
weeklyScds.tpd_ass_en:
Learning Instructions

Students should examine the concept of creative destruction and innovation in global markets. The article introduces business strategies used by firms adapting to technological change.

Preliminary Homework

Read the article and identify key business strategies.

List vocabulary related to innovation and competition.

Learning Activities

Lecture on innovation and creative destruction.

Discussion on business strategy in global markets.

Group analysis of technological change.

weeklyScds.tpd_reading_en:
International Relations and Economic Cooperation
Reading
The Economist – International Section
Australia and Israel
weeklyScds.tpd_ass_en:
Learning Instructions

Students should analyze international economic cooperation and geopolitical relationships. Students should consider how political alliances influence economic partnerships.

Preliminary Homework

Read the article before class.

Identify examples of international cooperation.

Learning Activities

Lecture on geopolitics and international trade.

Group discussion on economic partnerships.

Student reflections on international relations.

weeklyScds.tpd_reading_en:
Global Trade and Supply Chain Challenges
Reading
The Economist (Selected article)
weeklyScds.tpd_ass_en:
Learning Instructions

Students should analyze current challenges in global supply chains and international logistics.

Learning Activities

Lecture on supply chain management.

Case discussion on global logistics.

Group analysis of trade disruptions.

weeklyScds.tpd_ass_en:
Specify job / Preliminary homework

Students should read the assigned article and watch the lecture video before the self-learning week. They should also prepare two questions related to the topic.

Learning activities / Learning tasks of self-learning week

Students will analyze the case study, participate in online discussion, and submit a short reflection report (300–500 words) summarizing their learning outcomes.

gradeRuleDescribe.course_pol_en: Students are expected to attend class regularly and participate actively in discussions and learning activities. Attendance is an important component of the course evaluation. Students should complete assigned readings before class and submit assignments on time. Late submissions may result in grade deductions unless prior approval is obtained from the instructor. During class, students should respect others’ opinions and maintain a professional and respectful learning environment. The use of digital devices should be related to course learning. Academic honesty must be observed at all times, and any form of plagiarism or cheating will not be tolerated.
gradeRuleDescribe.ais_meno_en: Students are expected to maintain the highest standards of academic integrity in this course. All submitted work must be the student’s own original work. Plagiarism, cheating, unauthorized collaboration, or the misuse of artificial intelligence tools is strictly prohibited. When external sources, including academic articles, online materials, or AI tools, are used, they must be properly cited and acknowledged. Any violation of academic integrity policies may result in penalties, including grade reduction or disciplinary action according to university regulations. Students are encouraged to engage in honest learning, critical thinking, and responsible academic conduct throughout the course.
